---
title: "Squeeze Harder, Say \"Same\": Physical Effort Shifts Older Adults' Perceptual Criterion"
abstract: |
  Perception in daily life often takes place while the body is working, and combining demands is more costly with age. Whether physical effort changes what older adults perceive or only how readily they report a change, and whether pupil size tracks that effect, is unknown. Sixty-eight older adults judged whether two tones or two visual gratings were the same or different while holding a handgrip at low (5%) or high (40%) physical effort, with pupil diameter recorded throughout, and all trials were analyzed with mixed-effects models. Under high physical effort, participants reported a difference less often, and the reduction on trials with identical stimuli was similar in size, although uncertain on its own, which is consistent with a conservative shift in the criterion for reporting a difference. The reduction was slightly larger for the smallest differences, but sensitivity did not decline overall, in line with an earlier per-participant analysis of the same cohort. Pupil size during the grip differed little between physical effort levels. The pupil response after the second stimulus (the probe) was smaller under high physical effort, but the grip was released during that interval. A larger pupil just before the probe was weakly associated with lower sensitivity, and the response after it was not. In older adults, physical effort appears to change mainly how readily a difference is reported rather than how well it is perceived, and pupil size did not account for that change.

```{r setup}
insert_block_rules <- function(tab, block_rows) {
  lines <- strsplit(as.character(tab), "\n", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
  lastfoot <- which(grepl("\\\\endlastfoot$", lines))
  if (length(lastfoot) == 1L) {
    data_idx <- which(seq_along(lines) > lastfoot[[1]] & grepl("\\\\\\\\$", lines))
  } else {
    mid <- which(grepl("\\\\midrule$", lines))
    bottom <- which(grepl("\\\\bottomrule$", lines))
    if (length(mid) < 1L || length(bottom) < 1L) {
      stop("fixed-effects table did not have a header rule", call. = FALSE)
    }
    data_idx <- which(
      seq_along(lines) > mid[[1]] &
        seq_along(lines) < bottom[[length(bottom)]] &
        grepl("\\\\\\\\$", lines)
    )
  }
  if (sum(block_rows) != length(data_idx)) {
    stop("block sizes do not match the fixed-effects rows", call. = FALSE)
  }
  ends <- cumsum(block_rows)
  ends <- ends[-length(ends)]
  for (k in rev(ends)) {
    lines <- append(lines, "\\midrule", after = data_idx[[k]])
  }
  paste(lines, collapse = "\n")
}

    plain <- names(df)
    plain <- gsub("\\\\shortstack\\{", "", plain)
    plain <- gsub("\\\\\\\\", " ", plain)
    plain <- gsub("\\}", "", plain)
    plain <- gsub("\\\\%", "%", plain)
    if ("Statistic" %in% names(df)) {
      df$Statistic <- sub("^z = ", "*z* = ", df$Statistic)
      df$Statistic <- sub("^t\\(", "*t*(", df$Statistic)
    }
    plain <- ifelse(plain %in% c("p", "N", "M", "SD", "n"), paste0("*", plain, "*"), plain)
    names(df) <- plain
    return(knitr::kable(df))
  }
  stopifnot(length(widths) == ncol(df))
  df[] <- lapply(df, style_stat_latex)
  nms <- names(df)
  nms <- latex_escape(nms)
  nms[nms %in% c("p", "N", "M", "SD", "n")] <- paste0("$", nms[nms %in% c("p", "N", "M", "SD", "n")], "$")
  names(df) <- nms
  tab <- knitr::kable(
    df,
    format = "latex",
    booktabs = TRUE,
    longtable = TRUE,
    align = widths,
    escape = FALSE,
    linesep = ""
  )
  tab <- sub(
    "\\begin{longtable}",
    paste0("\\begingroup\\setlength{\\tabcolsep}{", tabcolsep, "}", size, "\\begin{longtable}"),
    tab,
    fixed = TRUE
  )
  tab <- sub("\\end{longtable}", "\\end{longtable}\\endgroup", tab, fixed = TRUE)
  if (!is.null(block_rows)) tab <- insert_block_rules(tab, block_rows)
  knitr::asis_output(tab)
}

    check.names = FALSE,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE

}
```

# Introduction

Everyday perception often takes place while the body is working, which combines two demands: the physical effort of a motor task and the task difficulty of a perceptual judgment. Older adults show larger dual-task costs than younger adults [@verhaeghen2003], and holding an effortful isometric grip lowered older adults' visual working-memory accuracy when distractors were present [@azer2023]. What physical effort does to a perceptual judgment, and whether its effect depends on task difficulty, is less clear.

A psychometric function relates the size of the difference between two stimuli, here called the offset, to the probability of reporting "different." Its slope indexes sensitivity, how sharply that probability rises with the offset, and catch trials, on which the two stimuli are identical, show how often a difference is reported when there is none. Physical effort could change the function in two ways [@macmillan2005detection; @prins2016psychophysics]. If the sensory evidence becomes noisier, sensitivity falls and the function becomes shallower; physical effort would then degrade what older adults perceive. If observers instead require more evidence before reporting a difference, the criterion shifts: the function moves toward larger offsets without becoming shallower, and "different" responses also become rarer on catch trials. Physical effort would then change how readily older adults report a difference, not what they perceive.

A capacity account holds that concurrent demands compete for limited processing resources [@kahneman1973; @wickens2008]. If a difficult judgment and high physical effort draw on the same resources, the cost of physical effort should be largest when the judgment is hardest, here at the smallest offsets, and absent on catch trials, where there is no difference to miss. Chapter 1 [@dastgheib_inpress_effects] tested this account in younger adults performing a working-memory task and two discrimination tasks, one auditory and one visual. Harder trials were less accurate in every task and slower in both discrimination tasks, high physical effort slowed responses only in the visual discrimination task, and task difficulty and physical effort did not interact on any measure. Whether the same holds in older adults has not been tested.

Pupil size increases with task difficulty [@beatty1982; @vanderwel2018] and with physical effort [@zenon2014], so it can register both demands. In older adults the pupil is smaller and its range of dilation is narrower [@winn1994; @piquado2010], so effects of either demand may be harder to detect. In Chapter 1, high physical effort enlarged the pupil response in all three tasks, task difficulty did not change the whole-trial pupil response, and the two did not interact. Pupil size just before a stimulus reflects the state in which the observer meets it and has been linked to task engagement and performance [@gilzenrat2010; @murphy2011]. The task-evoked pupil response (TEPR) follows the stimulus and partly reflects the decision itself, so its association with the judgment is harder to interpret.

In the older adults studied here, @sun2026handgrip fitted a psychometric function to each participant and found that high physical effort raised thresholds, the offset needed to report "different" on a set proportion of trials, without changing slopes, which they interpreted as a more conservative criterion. With 75 trials per physical effort level, however, a single participant's slope is uncertain, and that analysis did not relate the effect of physical effort to the pupil, which Sun et al. identified as the next step. A model of all trials, with participants as random effects, estimates directly how the effect of physical effort changes across offsets, and it can relate pupil size on each trial to the judgment on that trial.

This chapter asks two questions. The first is how high physical effort changes the judgment. The criterion account predicts fewer "different" responses by a similar amount at every offset and on catch trials, the sensitivity account predicts a shallower function, and the capacity account predicts a reduction that is largest at the smallest offsets and absent on catch trials. In a probit model of all trials, these predictions correspond to a physical effort effect that is the same across offsets and on catch trials, a negative offset × physical effort interaction, and a positive offset × physical effort interaction (@fig-effort-by-offset, panel A). The second question is whether pupil size tracks these effects: whether it differs between physical effort levels during the grip and after the probe, whether the TEPR differs with offset, and whether pupil size just before the probe tracks the slope of the judgment from trial to trial.

# Methods

## Participants and trials {#sec-participants}

Recruitment, exclusions, and demographics are those of @sun2026handgrip. Participants gave written informed consent and were paid, and procedures were approved by the University of California, Riverside Institutional Review Board. The behavioral analysis uses the cleaned trial file of that study: `r v_int("m1_nobs")` trials from `r v_int("m1_n_participants")` participants (`r v_int("m1_n_adt")` auditory, `r v_int("m1_n_vdt")` visual), of whom `r v_words("n_one_task")` completed only one task (@tbl-demographics). In that file, trials were excluded when grip force was not maintained within the target range (1–15% of MVC for low physical effort, 30–55% for high physical effort) for at least two-thirds of the 2- to 3-s period after trial onset, or when the response was missing, implausibly fast, or part of a run with more than 90% identical responses; about 90% of trials remained [@sun2026handgrip].

The pupil analyses use a subset of these trials: those with a recording that passed the checks described under Pupillometry (@sec-pupillometry). The task-evoked models (M3 and M4) use `r v_int("m3_nobs")` trials from `r v_int("m3_n_participants")` participants (`r v_int("m3_n_adt")` auditory, `r v_int("m3_n_vdt")` visual), and the grip-period model (M2) uses `r v_int("m2_nobs")` trials from `r v_int("m2_n_participants")` participants. Of the `r v_int("m1_n_participants")` participants, `r v_int("n_no_tepr")` contributed no trials to the task-evoked models because no recording existed or fewer than 20 trials passed the checks (@tbl-pupil-flow).

## Task, stimuli, and apparatus {#sec-task-paradigm}

Participants completed an auditory and a visual same–different task in the scanner, one task per session, in counterbalanced order. The tasks were adapted from the auditory and visual discrimination tasks of Chapter 1, with different offsets and timing. On each trial they held a left-hand grip at 5% (low physical effort) or 40% (high physical effort) of their maximum voluntary contraction (MVC), heard or saw a standard and then a comparison stimulus, the probe (the target in Chapter 1), judged whether the two were the same or different, and rated their confidence (@fig-paradigm). The inter-trial interval was 1.5–4.5 s. From squeeze onset, the standard began at 3.75 s and the probe at 4.35 s, each lasting 0.1 s. At probe offset (4.45 s), a change in border color cued participants to release the grip. The same–different response window ran from 4.70 to 7.70 s, and the confidence window followed. Each task had five blocks of 30 trials, in which the five probe levels and the two physical effort levels were crossed, three trials per combination, in pseudorandom order.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
#| out-width: "75%"
#| fig-align: center

stopifnot(file.exists(paradigm_path))
knitr::include_graphics(paradigm_path)
```

The auditory standard was a 1,000-Hz tone, and the probe was identical or 8, 16, 32, or 64 Hz higher. The visual standard was a Gabor patch (1.5 cycles/degree, Michelson contrast 0.20, 4°), and the probe was identical or had a contrast 0.06, 0.12, 0.24, or 0.48 higher. Trials with an identical probe are catch trials.

Stimuli were presented with Psychtoolbox 3.0.18 [@brainard1997] in MATLAB R2022b on a PROPixx projector (VPixx Technologies; 480 Hz, 1920 × 1080) viewed through a head-coil mirror (effective viewing distance 12 cm), and sounds were delivered through MRI-compatible earbuds. Grip force was recorded with an MRI-compatible dynamometer (Current Designs; 100 Hz) and pupil diameter with a TRACKPixx binocular eye tracker (VPixx Technologies; 2,000 Hz). MVC was the mean of three maximal squeezes, measured in an initial session outside the scanner and again in the scanner, and the value measured in the scanner set the 5% and 40% targets.

## Pupillometry {#sec-pupillometry}

Blinks and other artifacts were removed with ET-Remove-Artifacts [@mather2020isometric]. Pupil diameter, in arbitrary units, was analyzed at 250 Hz on a time axis that starts 3 s before squeeze onset; trials whose recording did not match that axis were excluded (@sec-supp-models). Four measures were taken from each trial. The pre-squeeze baseline is the mean over the 0.5 s before squeeze onset. The grip-period mean is the mean over 1.0–4.35 s after squeeze onset, minus the pre-squeeze baseline. Pre-probe pupil is the mean over the 0.5 s before probe onset (3.85–4.35 s); because this window follows the standard (3.75–3.85 s), it contains the early response to the standard. The TEPR is the mean over 4.65–7.65 s minus pre-probe pupil. Each measure required at least half of its samples to be valid, and a participant entered a pupil model only with at least 20 such trials in that task.

The TEPR window begins after probe offset, so grip release, the release cue, the response screen, and the button press all fall inside it. Of the four measures, only pre-probe pupil precedes the probe.

In the models that relate pupil size to the judgment, each pupil measure was split into a state and a trait component within that model's sample. State is the trial value minus the participant's mean for that task, divided by the standard deviation pooled across participant × task cells, so its coefficient reflects trial-to-trial fluctuation. Trait is the participant's mean for that task on the same scale.

## Models {#sec-models}

The behavioral outcome was a "different" response. Catch was coded 1 on catch trials and 0 on trials with a nonzero offset, so the reference is the average nonzero offset. Centered offset was −1.5, −0.5, 0.5, and 1.5 on the four nonzero offsets and 0 on catch trials. Physical effort (low, 5% of MVC; high, 40% of MVC) and task (auditory, visual) were sum-coded, low = −0.5 and high = +0.5, auditory = −0.5 and visual = +0.5. A sum-coded coefficient is the difference between the two levels on the model's link scale, high minus low for physical effort and visual minus auditory for task, and neither factor has a reference level.

Models were fit in R [@R] with lme4 `r v("lme4_version")` and lmerTest `r v("lmerTest_version")` [@bates2015; @kuznetsova2017lmerTest]. Each started from the maximal random-effects structure [@barr2013] and was simplified in fixed steps until the fit was neither singular nor flagged by the optimizer [@bates2015]; the steps are listed in @sec-supp-models. The models were specified before they were fit; the study was not pre-registered, and the reading of the sign of the offset × physical effort interaction as a test of the capacity account was added after the results were known (@sec-disc-criterion).

**Behavior (M1).** All `r v_int("m1_nobs")` trials were analyzed with a probit regression of "different" responses on catch, centered offset, physical effort, and task. The interactions were catch × physical effort, offset × physical effort, catch × task, offset × task, physical effort × task, catch × physical effort × task, and offset × physical effort × task. Each participant had a random slope for catch, centered offset, physical effort, and task. Because the centered offset is 0 both on catch trials and at the average nonzero offset, the physical effort coefficient is the effect of physical effort at the average offset, and the catch × physical effort interaction is how much the effect on catch trials differs from it. The criterion account predicts a negative physical effort coefficient and no catch × physical effort interaction. The sign of the offset × physical effort interaction separates the sensitivity account (negative) from the capacity account (positive).

**Grip-period pupil (M2).** Linear model of the grip-period mean on physical effort, task, and a physical effort × task interaction, with a by-participant random slope for physical effort. It tests whether high physical effort enlarged the pupil during the grip. The reported manipulation check is grip force, not pupil [@sun2026handgrip].

**Task-evoked pupil (M3).** Linear model of the TEPR mean on physical effort, task, and a physical effort × task interaction, and on catch and centered offset, with by-participant random slopes for physical effort and offset. It tests whether the TEPR differed with physical effort and with offset.

**Pupil and sensitivity (M4).** Probit models on the same `r v_int("m4a_nobs")` trials as M3. The primary predictor is pre-probe pupil (M4a). The secondary predictor is the TEPR mean (M4b). Both include state and trait, and both keep physical effort and task so the pupil coefficients are estimated within levels of physical effort and task. The state interactions are offset × state (the slope term) and catch × state. A negative slope term means a shallower function.

**Missing pupil data (M5).** A control model tested whether pupil data were more often usable at one physical effort level (@sec-supp-pupil).

## Statistical inference {#sec-inference}

Effects are reported with Wald 95% confidence intervals and two-sided *p* values; for the linear models, degrees of freedom are Satterthwaite approximations. No correction was applied across models, because each model tests a different question. No equivalence bound was set, so a nonsignificant effect is reported as its estimate and interval, not as evidence that there was no effect.

# Results

## Physical effort and "different" responses {#sec-behavior}

Under high physical effort, the mean proportion of "different" responses was lower at every offset in both tasks except the 0.24 contrast offset in the visual task (@fig-p-diff). On catch trials, the proportion of "different" responses was `r v("catch_adt_p")` in the auditory task and `r v("catch_vdt_p")` in the visual task. Responding was near ceiling at the largest offset (auditory, `r v("top_adt_p")`; visual, `r v("top_vdt_p")`), where the high-minus-low difference in proportion was `r v("level4_adt_diff_prop")` in the auditory task and `r v("level4_vdt_diff_prop")` in the visual task.

```{r}
#| label: fig-p-diff
```

# Discussion

We asked whether high physical effort changes older adults' perceptual judgments by lowering sensitivity or by shifting the criterion for reporting a difference, and whether pupil size tracks either effect. Under high physical effort, older adults reported a difference less often in both tasks, by a similar amount on catch trials as at the average offset, although the catch-trial estimate was uncertain on its own, and the psychometric function did not become shallower. The reduction was slightly larger at the smallest offsets. Pupil size during the grip differed little between physical effort levels, the TEPR was smaller under high physical effort, and only pupil size before the probe was associated, weakly, with sensitivity.

## Criterion, not sensitivity {#sec-disc-criterion}

The reduction on catch trials was similar in size to the reduction at the average offset, the pattern the criterion account predicts, and the function did not become shallower, contrary to the sensitivity account [@macmillan2005detection]. The catch trials, however, do not separate the criterion account from the capacity account. Taken alone, the reduction on catch trials had an interval that included zero (@fig-effort-by-offset, panel B), and the interval of the catch × physical effort interaction also includes the value the capacity account predicts, no reduction on catch trials. The criterion reading therefore rests on the direction and size of the catch-trial estimate together with converging evidence from the same cohort, in which per-participant psychometric functions showed higher thresholds and unchanged slopes [@sun2026handgrip].

The effect of physical effort was largest at the smallest offsets and close to zero at the largest, a positive offset × physical effort interaction (@fig-effort-by-offset, panel B). That is the direction the capacity account predicts, but the cost was small and its interval nearly reached zero. The increase across offsets appears steeper in the visual task than in the auditory task, but the offset × physical effort × task interaction was not significant (@sec-supp-models). Two further cautions apply. The analysis plan specified this term as a test of a shallower function, and reading a positive term as support for the capacity account was added after the results were known. In addition, responding was near ceiling at the largest offset, where a probit model without a lapse rate can express a shrinking difference as a steeper slope. Taken together, the data favor a criterion shift over a loss of sensitivity, with at most a small additional cost on the hardest judgments. Chapter 1 [@dastgheib_inpress_effects] found no interaction between task difficulty and physical effort in younger adults, but without a younger group these data cannot show whether the small cost reflects age.

## Why the criterion shifts {#sec-disc-why}

Three explanations could account for the criterion shift. The first places it in the decision: under a concurrent physical demand, observers may require more evidence before reporting a change. In the same cohort, high physical effort also improved metacognitive efficiency, an effect that appeared to be driven by lower confidence on errors at the easiest auditory offset [@sun2026handgrip]. A decision state that is both more conservative and better at registering its own errors fits a criterion shift better than degraded input, although the two physical effort effects did not covary across participants [@sun2026handgrip], so they may not share one mechanism. The second is that physical effort acts on the decision through processes indexed by the pupil. Phasic pupil responses have been associated with smaller choice biases [@deGee2020pupil], but here neither pre-probe pupil nor the TEPR predicted the rate of "different" responses, so trial-to-trial changes in pupil size did not carry the physical effort effect. The third places the shift at the response. "Different" was always reported with the right index finger and "same" with the right middle finger, and a left-hand grip could bias right-hand responding toward one finger. Choices alone cannot separate these explanations. Chapter 3 uses response times to test whether the shift lies in how the evidence is evaluated, in how much evidence is required, or in a bias set before the stimulus.

## Physical effort and pupil size {#sec-disc-pupil}

Pupil size during the grip did not differ significantly between physical effort levels. In younger adults, by contrast, high physical effort enlarged the pupil response in every task (Chapter 1), although the measures are not directly comparable: Chapter 1 summarized the pupil from trial onset to the response window, including the response to the probe, and recorded it in a quiet, dimly lit laboratory rather than a scanner. Several features of this sample could weaken the effect. Older adults have smaller pupils and a narrower range of dilation [@winn1994; @piquado2010]. In the time course, the two physical effort levels separated only in the second half of the grip, and the separation persisted into the pre-probe window (@fig-pupil-timecourse), so a window that begins 1 s after squeeze onset also averages over a period in which they did not differ. The effect of physical effort also varied considerably across participants, and only `r v_int("m2_n_participants")` of the `r v_int("m1_n_participants")` participants contributed to that model.

The TEPR was smaller under high physical effort, but this difference cannot be attributed to processing of the probe. Grip release, its cue, and the button press fall inside the TEPR window, and releasing a grip held at high physical effort differs from releasing one held at low physical effort. The TEPR is also measured from pre-probe pupil, which the time course shows was larger under high physical effort, and evoked responses tend to be smaller when baseline pupil size is larger [@gilzenrat2010]; in the time course, the two physical effort levels converged after the probe (@fig-pupil-timecourse). The TEPR did not differ with offset or on catch trials, just as task difficulty did not change the whole-trial pupil response in Chapter 1.

## Pre-probe pupil and sensitivity {#sec-disc-preprobe}

On trials on which pupil size before the probe was larger than the participant's mean, the psychometric function was shallower. The evidence is weak: the interval reaches zero, and the pre-probe window contains the early response to the standard. One interpretation comes from adaptive gain theory, which links pupil size to the activity of the locus coeruleus–noradrenergic (LC–NE) system [@astonjones2005; @joshi2016]. In that theory, a larger baseline pupil accompanies a less task-focused state [@gilzenrat2010], and performance is best at intermediate baseline pupil sizes [@murphy2011]. Isometric handgrip engages the noradrenergic system [@mather2020isometric], and the locus coeruleus is among the brain structures most vulnerable to aging [@mather2016], so a route from physical effort to perception through the LC–NE system is plausible in older adults. This study, however, neither manipulated nor measured locus coeruleus activity during the task, and pupil size also covaries with activity outside the locus coeruleus [@joshi2016]. The association is therefore a hypothesis for a study with a pre-stimulus baseline free of other stimuli, not a finding this chapter rests on. The TEPR, summarized as a mean or as an area (@sec-supp-robust), was associated with neither the slope nor the rate of "different" responses.

## Limitations {#sec-disc-limits}

Several limitations qualify these conclusions. The pupil windows were constrained by the trial sequence: grip release, its cue, and the button press fall inside the task-evoked window, and the pre-probe window contains the early response to the standard. The response mapping was not counterbalanced, so a bias tied to one finger cannot be ruled out. With two physical effort levels, the data cannot describe a dose–response relation or test an inverted-U relation between physical effort and performance. The chapter has no younger group, so no effect can be attributed to age. Locus coeruleus activity was not measured. Data were collected in an MRI scanner, which constrains luminance, posture, and noise, and pupil size was recorded in arbitrary units. Pupil data were missing or unusable for `r v_int("n_no_tepr")` of the `r v_int("m1_n_participants")` participants, and trials at high physical effort were slightly more likely to be usable (@sec-supp-pupil), although every pupil model included physical effort. In the models that related pupil size to the judgment (M4a and M4b), the physical effort terms had the same sign as in M1, but their intervals included zero (@sec-supp-models). The behavioral model had no lapse rate, so the positive offset × physical effort interaction cannot be separated from a ceiling effect.

## Conclusion {#sec-disc-conclusion}

For older adults, high physical effort appears to change mainly how readily a difference is reported rather than how well it is perceived, and its cost depended little on task difficulty. That distinction matters wherever older adults must notice a change while exerting themselves: a more conservative criterion predicts more missed changes when the evidence is weak, without implying that perception itself is impaired. A study that counterbalances the response mapping, uses more than two physical effort levels, measures a pre-stimulus baseline free of other stimuli, and models confidence alongside choice could separate the decision and response explanations and test whether pupil size before a stimulus predicts discrimination. In this chapter, high physical effort made older adults less likely to report a difference, in a pattern that favors a criterion shift toward "same," and pupil size did not account for that change.

## Model estimation {#sec-supp-models}

Each trial was epoched from 3 s before squeeze onset at 250 Hz, so sample $k$ falls at $t_k = -3 + 0.004(k - 1)$ s. A trial was retained when it had 3,425 or 3,426 samples and its median time step was within $10^{-6}$ of 0.004 s. All models used the bobyqa optimizer with a maximum of 200,000 function evaluations. A fit was accepted only when it was not singular and the optimizer returned no convergence message. If the maximal model failed that rule, the random-effects structure was reduced in fixed steps: correlated slopes, then uncorrelated slopes, then removal of the random slope with the smallest variance, then a random intercept only (@tbl-reduction).

```{=latex}
\Needspace{12\baselineskip}
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-reduction
#| tbl-cap: "Random-effects steps for each model. A step is accepted when the fit is not singular and the optimizer returns no convergence message."

red <- read_export("tbl_reduction.csv")
stopifnot(nrow(red) > 0L)
step_lab <- c(
  "1_maximal" = "Maximal",
  "2_uncorrelated" = "Uncorrelated slopes",
  "3_drop_b1_state" = "Drop pre-probe slope",
  "3_drop_tepr_state" = "Drop task-evoked slope",
  "specified_intercept" = "Intercept only",
  "same_as_M4b_3_drop_tepr_state" = "As accepted for the task-evoked model",
  "D-S1_drop_x_c" = "Drop offset slope"
)
re_lab <- c(
  "(1 + catch + x_c + effort_c + task_c | subject)" = "Intercept and slopes for catch, offset, physical effort, and task",
  "(1 + effort_c | subject)" = "Intercept and a slope for physical effort",
  "(1 + effort_c + x_c | subject)" = "Intercept and slopes for physical effort and offset",
  "(1 + catch + x_c + b1_state | subject)" = "Intercept and correlated slopes for catch, offset, and pre-probe pupil",
  "(1 + catch + x_c + b1_state || subject)" = "Intercept and uncorrelated slopes for catch, offset, and pre-probe pupil",
  "(1 + catch + x_c || subject)" = "Intercept and uncorrelated slopes for catch and offset",
  "(1 + catch + x_c + tepr_state | subject)" = "Intercept and correlated slopes for catch, offset, and the task-evoked response",
  "(1 + catch + x_c + tepr_state || subject)" = "Intercept and uncorrelated slopes for catch, offset, and the task-evoked response",
  "(1 | subject)" = "Intercept only",
  "(1 + catch || subject)" = "Intercept and an uncorrelated slope for catch"
)
stopifnot(all(red$Step %in% names(step_lab)))
stopifnot(all(red[["Random effects"]] %in% names(re_lab)))
conv <- red$Convergence
conv_lab <- ifelse(
  is.na(conv) | conv %in% c("NULL", ""),
  "None",
  ifelse(
    grepl("isSingular", conv, fixed = TRUE),
    "Boundary",
    ifelse(grepl("failed to converge", conv, fixed = TRUE), "Did not converge", NA_character_)
  )
)
stopifnot(!anyNA(conv_lab))
yn <- function(x) ifelse(as.logical(x), "Yes", "No")
display <- data.frame(
  Model = red$Model,
  Step = unname(step_lab[red$Step]),
  "Random effects" = unname(re_lab[red[["Random effects"]]]),
  Singular = yn(red$Singular),
  Convergence = conv_lab,
  Accepted = yn(red$Accepted),
  check.names = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
display$Model <- id_display(display$Model)
if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
  display$Convergence <- ifelse(
    display$Convergence == "Did not converge",
    "\\mbox{Did not converge}",
    display$Convergence
  )
  knitr::kable(
    display,
    format = "latex",
    booktabs = TRUE,
    longtable = TRUE,
    escape = FALSE,
    linesep = "",
    align = c(
      ">{\\raggedright\\arraybackslash}p{0.48in}",
      ">{\\raggedright\\arraybackslash}p{1.28in}",
      ">{\\raggedright\\arraybackslash}p{2.05in}",
      ">{\\centering\\arraybackslash}p{0.52in}",
      ">{\\raggedright\\arraybackslash}p{1.22in}",
      ">{\\centering\\arraybackslash}p{0.52in}"
    )
  )
} else {
  knitr::kable(display)
}
```

## Robustness {#sec-supp-robust}

The primary TEPR summary is the mean rather than the area under the curve, because on these trials the area tracks the mean multiplied by the proportion of valid samples.

R1 replaces the TEPR mean in M4b with the gap-respecting area. M4b's accepted random-effects structure did not converge for that outcome (maximum absolute gradient `r fmt_sig(as.numeric(v("s1_max_abs_grad")), 2)` against lme4's default tolerance of 0.002). The ladder was continued from that structure by dropping the offset random slope. That step was accepted (`r v_int("s1_nobs")` trials). The offset × state term was `r v("s1_x_c_teprauc_state_est")` (SE `r v("s1_x_c_teprauc_state_se")`), 95% CI `r v("s1_x_c_teprauc_state_ci")`, *p* `r S1_slope$p_fmt`. The state term was `r v("s1_teprauc_state_est")`, *p* `r S1_state$p_fmt`, and the catch × state term was `r v("s1_catch_teprauc_state_est")`, *p* `r S1_catch$p_fmt`. The area version agrees with M4b in the sense that none of these intervals excludes zero. M4b itself was not changed.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="dissertation"}

```{=latex}
\Needspace{12\baselineskip}
```

## Additional estimation checks (dissertation only)

M1, M4a, and M4b were re-estimated with the optimizers that ship with lme4 (`r v("allfit_optimizers")`). No key-term estimate from a converged optimizer differed from the accepted bobyqa estimate by more than 0.01. The largest absolute key-term deviation in that set was `r v("allfit_max_abs_dev")`.

R2 fits M1's formula to the `r v_int("s2_nobs")` trials from the `r v_int("s2_n_participants")` participants who contributed to the TEPR sample. The maximal model was singular, so it was not accepted. The point estimates were `r v("s2_effort_c_est")` for physical effort (*p* `r S2_effort$p_fmt`), `r v("s2_catch_effort_c_est")` for catch × physical effort (*p* `r S2_catch$p_fmt`), and `r v("s2_x_c_effort_c_est")` for offset × physical effort (*p* `r S2_slope$p_fmt`). They are reported only to show the direction in this subset. They are not a second accepted test.

```{=latex}
\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{12\baselineskip}
```

## Analysis provenance (dissertation only)

Recordings are the December 21 processing of the same sessions. The December 25 processing added no participant who was absent from December 21, so it is not in these models.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{14\baselineskip}
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-axis
#| tbl-cap: "Checks that the December 21 recordings are on a 250 Hz axis."

axis_tab <- read_export("tbl_axis.csv")
stopifnot(identical(axis_tab$Test, c("T1 within-trial step", "T2 phase labels", "T3 December 21 vs 25")))
axis_num <- function(note, pattern) {
  hit <- regexec(pattern, note, perl = TRUE)
  parts <- regmatches(note, hit)[[1]]
  if (length(parts) < 2L) stop("axis note is missing an exported number", call. = FALSE)
  as.numeric(parts[2])
}
t1 <- axis_num(axis_tab$Note[1], "= ([0-9.]+)\\s*$")
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(t1, 1)))
t2_dur <- axis_num(axis_tab$Note[2], "duration ([0-9.]+) s")
t2_len <- axis_num(axis_tab$Note[2], "length ([0-9.]+) samples")
t3_b <- axis_num(axis_tab$Note[3], "b = ([0-9.]+)")
t3_r <- axis_num(axis_tab$Note[3], "r at b = 1 = ([0-9.]+)")
r_txt <- sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", t3_r))
if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
  note3 <- sprintf(
    "Median index scale \\textit{b} = %.3f; median \\textit{r} at \\textit{b} = 1: %s",
    t3_b, r_txt
  )
  n_name <- "\\textit{n}"
} else {
  note3 <- sprintf(
    "Median index scale *b* = %.3f; median *r* at *b* = 1: %s",
    t3_b, r_txt
  )
  n_name <- "*n*"
}
axis_show <- data.frame(
  Test = c(
    "Within-trial time step",
    "Squeeze-gauge duration",
    "Agreement with December 25 processing"
  ),
  n = format(axis_tab$n, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE, scientific = FALSE),
  "Implied step (s)" = {
    step <- as.numeric(axis_tab[["Implied step"]])
    stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(step[1], 0.004)), isTRUE(all.equal(step[2], 0.004)))
    c(formatC(step[1:2], format = "f", digits = 3), "\u2014")
  },
  Note = c(
    "Median step of 0.004 s in every trial",
    sprintf("%g s; median %g samples", t2_dur, t2_len),
    note3
  ),
  check.names = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
names(axis_show)[names(axis_show) == "n"] <- n_name
if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
  knitr::kable(
    axis_show,
    format = "latex",
    booktabs = TRUE,
    longtable = TRUE,
    escape = FALSE,
    align = c(
      ">{\\raggedright\\arraybackslash}p{2.15in}",
      ">{\\centering\\arraybackslash}p{0.45in}",
      ">{\\centering\\arraybackslash}p{1.05in}",
      ">{\\raggedright\\arraybackslash}p{2.45in}"
    )
  )
} else {
  knitr::kable(axis_show)
}
```
